question: In 2019, administrative rules in Idaho ceased to be automatically reauthorised, meaning that the authorities have to actively justify and reissue any regulations that are to be maintained. The model was subsequently formalised as ‘zero-based regulation’, involving regular reviews of the rules and regulations in place.

By the end of 2024, around 3 235 pages of rules had been abolished, representing around 38 % compared with 20181. As part of the competitiveness agenda, the Commission has set targets to cut red tape by 25 % for businesses in general and by 35 % for SMEs, for example using Omnibus packages, REFIT and the ‘one in, one out’ approach2.
The Draghi report also points out that the regulatory burden is an obstacle to Europe’s competitiveness3. 1.
Has the Commission studied Idaho’s model or other systems with automatic sunset clauses and mandatory reviews of existing legislation?
Does the Commission intend to propose or pilot a mechanism whereby parts of the EU’s regulatory framework will have to be regularly reassessed and actively justified in order to remain in force?

What specific steps does the Commission intend to take to move from the simplification of individual rules to a real zero-based or regulatory budgeting approach for all the rules and regulations in place in the EU?

According to the Idaho Governor’s Office and a subsequent assessment of zero-based regulation, 3 235 pages of rules had been abolished by the end of 2024, around 38 % compared with 2018. 2 The Commission’s competitiveness and simplification agenda includes targets of cutting red tape by at least 25 % for businesses in general and by 35 % for SMEs.

The Commission’s current ‘one in, one out’ approach offsets costs but does not automatically repeal existing legislation. 3 The Draghi report, ‘The Future of European Competitiveness’, section on the simplification of rules. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.11.2026) The Commission is committed to promoting future-proof and adaptive regulation by proposing the introduction of monitoring, evaluation and sunset clauses in new legislation where relevant, so that outdated or unnecessary rules do not stay in force.

The Commission outlined this pledge in its Communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’ adopted in April 20261. At the same time, the Commission is also committed to providing businesses and public authorities the high level of regulatory certainty and stability that they require.

In addition, the Commission is screening existing EU rules to eliminate unnecessary burdens, regulatory inconsistencies and overlaps, and has also committed to gradually consolidating EU rules to reduce regulatory fragmentation, including in the 12 priority areas identified in its Action Plan on Regulatory Deep Cleaning2. ‘Making it easier to do business in Europe’ is a key priority to ensure EU’s competitiveness.

So far, the Commission has adopted simplification measures since the start of the mandate which reduce administrative burden by approximately EUR 22.3 billion, contributing to the target of reducing the administrative burden arising from the EU acquis by at least 25%.
In the 2026 State of the Union address3 and in the Letter of Intent4, the President of the Commission announced additional simplification packages in the areas of banking, transport and housing.

Moreover, co-legislators also have a central role to play, including when it comes to embedding the principles of regulatory discipline and simplicity by design in future legislation, and assessing the impacts of their substantial amendments.
